explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count messages enabled for every statement, adding network chatter for callers.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF while the procedure uses explicit transactions allows run-time errors to leave a transaction open and partially applied.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders returns every column including three nvarchar(max) columns and couples callers to future schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so the returned rows are arbitrary.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders and already unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) in the WHERE clause prevents a range seek on OrderDate; use OrderDate >= '20160101' AND OrderDate < '20170101'.
The year 2016 is hard-coded in the predicate rather than supplied as a parameter.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces an implicit conversion that can hurt the FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID index seek.
@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID produces a single plan that cannot seek efficiently for both cases.
LIKE N'%urgent%' on o.Comments has a leading wildcard and forces a full scan of the nvarchar(max) column.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices returns no rows if the subquery ever yields a NULL; NOT EXISTS is safer.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the indexed CustomerID column and makes the predicate non-sargable.
Customer identifier 1 is hard-coded in the predicate.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID applies arithmetic to the primary key column and prevents an index seek.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality that typically scans most of Sales.Orders.
Customer identifier 1 is hard-coded in the inequality predicate.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and multiplies the row counts.
SELECT TOP (1) over the Orders/Customers cross join has no ORDER BY, so the returned row is arbitrary.
Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines are listed with a comma and joined in WHERE instead of using ANSI JOIN syntax.
SELECT TOP (1) from the Orders/OrderLines join has no ORDER BY.
The COUNT(*) subquery on Sales.OrderLines executes once per Sales.Orders row; use a grouped join instead.
Correlated EXISTS on Sales.OrderLines per Orders row could be expressed as a set-based join.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL expression is duplicated in the select list and ORDER BY; reference the alias or a CTE instead.
ORDER BY 2 refers to a select-list position and breaks silently when columns are reordered.
OFFSET/FETCH ordered only by o.OrderDate has no unique tie-breaker, so pages can overlap or skip rows.
UNION between branches filtered on OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 performs needless duplicate removal; the sets are disjoint.
Order identifier 1 is hard-coded in the first UNION branch.
Order identifier 2 is hard-coded in the second UNION branch.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts every line when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
The COUNT(*) subquery against Sales.OrderLines is evaluated per outer Orders row.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID from all of Sales.Orders silently assigns the last of many rows.
Table variable @OrderIds has no statistics and can receive poor cardinality estimates.
INSERT ... SELECT TOP (5) from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so arbitrary OrderIDs are captured.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table schema implicitly instead of declaring it.
SELECT TOP (5) INTO #ImplicitOrders has no ORDER BY.
#ImplicitOrders is created but never dropped before the procedure ends.
order_cursor with OPEN/FETCH NEXT processes Sales.Orders rows one at a time.
Cursor query SELECT TOP (2) from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY.
WHILE loop on @Counter performs iterative processing instead of a set-based operation.
@CustomerID is converted and concatenated into the SQL string instead of being bound as a parameter.
EXEC (@Sql) runs concatenated SQL with no parameterization, defeating plan reuse.
@OrderID is concatenated into the SQL text rather than passed via sp_executesql parameters.
sys.sp_executesql is called without a parameter definition; the value is embedded in the string.
#Scratch is created but never dropped before the procedure ends.
CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows nor returns a failure status, hiding the error from the caller.
RAISERROR is used for a new error path; THROW is preferred.
PRINT output is buffered and not suitable for structured diagnostics.
Customer identifier 1 is hard-coded in the predicate on o.CustomerID.
Date constant '20160101' is embedded in the predicate without a named parameter or explanation.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') has no style parameter; the result depends on session DATEFORMAT/language.
COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the ON clause blocks index-based join optimization.
SELECT TOP (1) from the Orders/Invoices join has no ORDER BY.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on OrderID only to return o.OrderID, which is already available without the join.
SELECT TOP (1) from the Orders self-join has no ORDER BY.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts every order by an nvarchar(max) LOB column.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table with no restrictive WHERE clause.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 is a row-level filter that belongs in WHERE before grouping.
ORDER BY OrderCount on a single-row COUNT(*) aggregate is unnecessary.
MERGE on Sales.Orders has known concurrency and correctness edge cases; use separate UPDATE/INSERT logic.
MERGE sets target.Comments = target.Comments, writing no change but still logging and locking.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments changes no data but still incurs logging and locking.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 uses a broad non-key business value rather than a stable key.
Magic value -1 for Quantity is embedded in the DELETE predicate.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a worker thread inside the procedure.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not wrapped in BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH, so errors can leave it open.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session state and couples the procedure to identity management.
EXEC sp_who lacks the sys. schema qualifier, forcing a schema lookup.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is never reset to 0 and silently limits every subsequent statement in the session, including the later INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) has no explicit column list and depends on column order.
Category identifier 99 is hard-coded in the INSERT values.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers ... SELECT has no explicit column list.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' has a leading wildcard and cannot seek the UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL string.
User-supplied @CustomerName is embedded in the SQL text without parameterization, allowing SQL injection.
The dynamic LIKE pattern starts with % and forces a scan of #DemoCustomers.
sp_executesql is called with no parameter list; the value is already baked into @sql.
sp_executesql is called without the sys. schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and updates every row.
CustomerCategoryID value 1 is hard-coded in the UPDATE.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= ... filters the LEFT JOINed Sales.Orders table and silently converts the join to an inner join.
Date constant '2016-01-01' is embedded in the predicate without a parameter or label.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates true; use IS NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the select list executes row by row for every Sales.Customers row.
CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows nor returns a failure status.
CATCH block does not ROLLBACK the open transaction started on line 239 before handling the error.
WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers hard-codes an index choice and breaks if indexes change.
Three levels of nested derived tables (t1, t2, t3) over Sales.Customers should be flattened or rewritten as a CTE.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' has a leading wildcard and prevents an index seek on CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples the caller to every column the function returns.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti appears to be a multi-statement TVF, which has fixed cardinality estimates and cannot be inlined.
